t: Maximum Score After Binary Swaps — Heap Sweep Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem

Each `'1'` in `s` contributes the value at its current index. The only operation moves a `'1'` one step **left** across a `'0'`, so repeated operations let any `'1'` travel to *any* index less than or equal to its starting index (as long as the path is clear — other `'1'`s never block it because they also only move left, and two `'1'`s can never swap with each other). Note the score only depends on *which indices* hold a `'1'`, not on which original `'1'` got there.

**Example 1:** `nums = [2,1,5,2,3]`, `s = "01010"`. There are two ones at indices 1 and 3. Index 3's one can reach any of {0,1,2,3} and index 1's one any of {0,1}. The best placement is indices 0 and 2, giving `nums[0] + nums[2] = 2 + 5 = 7`.

**Example 2:** `s = "0000"` has no ones and no valid swaps exist, so the answer is 0.

With $n$ up to $10^5$, we need an $O(n \log n)$-style greedy rather than any state-space search.
k: A '1' at index j can ultimately occupy any index <= j, so the problem reduces to choosing a set of final positions dominated element-wise by the original one-positions.
Processing from right to left and giving each '1' the currently-largest unclaimed value (max-heap) is optimal by an exchange argument.
Scores can reach 10^5 * 10^9 = 10^14, so use 64-bit integers.

a.n: Approach 1: Right-to-left sweep with a max-heap
a.i: Scan from the rightmost index to the left. Maintain a max-heap of values of all indices seen so far (all indices `>= i`). Whenever we hit a `'1'` at index `i`, it may claim any free index `<= i`; assigning it the maximum value currently in the heap is safe: any optimal solution can be exchanged so this one takes that spot without loss. After processing all ones, the heap pops give exactly the optimal multiset of claimed values.
s: Initialize an empty max-heap (store negated values) and answer = 0.
Iterate i from n-1 down to 0; push nums[i] into the heap.
If s[i] == '1', pop the heap maximum and add it to the answer.
a.t: O(n log n) — each index is pushed once and popped at most once from the heap.
a.sp: O(n) — the heap holds at most all n values.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy by value with a Fenwick-tree feasibility check
a.i: View the final positions as a matching: sorted chosen positions $p_1 < \dots < p_m$ must satisfy $p_k \le q_k$ where $q_k$ are the sorted original one-positions. Feasible sets form a transversal matroid, so scanning indices in decreasing value order and taking an index whenever it keeps the set feasible yields the optimum. Feasibility of adding position $p$: the number of ones at indices `>= p` must exceed the number of already-chosen positions `>= p`, checked with a Fenwick tree plus a suffix count of ones.
s: Precompute suf[i] = number of '1' characters at indices >= i.
Sort all indices by nums value in decreasing order.
For each candidate position p in that order, check suf[p] - (chosenCount - fenwick.prefix(p-1)) > 0.
If feasible, add nums[p] to the answer, increment chosenCount, and update the Fenwick tree at p.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus O(log n) Fenwick updates/queries per index.
a.sp: O(n) — suffix counts, Fenwick tree, and the sorted index array.

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, lead with the observation that a `'1'` can move arbitrarily far left, then present the right-to-left max-heap sweep (Approach 1) — it is short, optimal, and easy to justify with an exchange argument. Mention Approach 2 to show matroid-style greedy reasoning if asked for alternatives.

**Pitfalls:** returning an `int` in Java/C++ (the answer can exceed 32-bit range); forgetting that ones cannot move right; assuming ones must stay in relative order matters — it does not, since only positions matter. **Edge cases:** all zeros (answer 0), all ones (answer is the full sum), single element. **Follow-ups:** what if a `'1'` could also move right (then the answer is simply the sum of the k largest values); what if each swap had a cost proportional to distance.
